title: DNA structure and replication
note: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands, with A pairing with T and G with C. Replication is semiconservative: each strand templates a new partner. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to a 3' end, so one strand is made continuously and the other in short Okazaki fragments.

read.title: Copying the code
text: Before a cell divides, it must copy all of its DNA accurately. Replication begins at sites called origins, where the two strands are opened into a pair of Y-shaped replication forks. Helicase unwinds the helix, single-strand binding proteins keep the strands apart, and topoisomerase relieves the twisting that builds up ahead of each fork.

DNA polymerase builds the new strands, but it has two limits. It cannot start a strand from nothing, so primase first lays down a short RNA primer. And it can add nucleotides only to a free 3' end, so new DNA always grows in the 5' to 3' direction.

Because the two template strands are antiparallel, these limits create an asymmetry. On the leading strand, the polymerase moves toward the fork and synthesizes continuously. On the lagging strand, it must work away from the fork, making short Okazaki fragments, each starting from its own primer. In bacteria, DNA polymerase I later replaces the primers with DNA, and ligase seals the pieces into one strand.
The result is two double helices, each containing one old strand and one new one. Polymerase proofreads as it goes, and repair enzymes fix most remaining errors.
